blocks.text: In a diesel engine the air in the cylinder is squeezed to about one-twentieth of its volume in a few milliseconds, too fast for much heat to escape, and its temperature rises enough to ignite sprayed fuel with no spark. The first law of thermodynamics turns that observation into a calculation.

blocks.markdown: The **first law for a closed system** says energy is conserved: the change in the system's total energy equals the net energy crossing its boundary as heat and work. For a stationary system with negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy only internal energy $U$ changes. Using the convention that heat $Q$ **into** the system is positive and work $W$ **done by** the system is positive:

blocks.caption: Closed system, stationary, units kJ; W includes all work modes, for example boundary work and shaft work

blocks.title: Internal energy
blocks.text: Internal energy $U$ (kJ) is the energy stored in the microscopic motion and interactions of the molecules. For an ideal gas it depends on temperature only, and for constant specific heat $\Delta U = m c_v \Delta T$ with $c_v$ the specific heat at constant volume (kJ/(kg K)). For air $c_v \approx 0.718$ kJ/(kg K) near room temperature (typical value).

blocks.markdown: The balance is an **accounting statement**. Heat and work are not properties; they are energy crossing the boundary, so a sign error is the commonest mistake. Check every term: if the gas receives work, then $W$ is negative; if the gas loses heat, then $Q$ is negative.

blocks.title: Piston-cylinder energy balance
blocks.prompt: A gas in a piston-cylinder device receives 120 kJ of heat from a burner while the piston lifts a load, so the gas does 45 kJ of work on the piston. Find the change in internal energy.

steps.text: State the balance with the signs: $Q=+120$ kJ in, $W=+45$ kJ out.

blocks.answer: The internal energy rises by 75 kJ; the gas gets hotter even though it did work.

blocks.markdown: Two special cases are especially useful. If the process is **adiabatic**, $Q=0$ and $\Delta U=-W$: all the work input becomes internal energy. If the volume is **constant**, there is no boundary work and $Q=\Delta U$: all the heat added goes to internal energy.

blocks.caption: How the balance simplifies for common processes

blocks.title: Adiabatic compression of air
blocks.prompt: 0.30 kg of air at 300 K is compressed in an insulated cylinder by a piston that does 40 kJ of work on the gas. Treat air as an ideal gas with constant cv = 0.718 kJ/(kg K). Find the final temperature.

steps.text: Adiabatic with work done on the gas.

blocks.answer: T2 is about 486 K. The result holds whether the compression is reversible or not, because only the work and the energy balance were used.

blocks.title: Heating air in a rigid tank
blocks.prompt: A rigid tank holds 1.5 kg of air at 290 K. Heat is added until the temperature reaches 400 K. Find the heat transferred.

steps.text: Rigid tank: no boundary work, so $W=0$ and $Q=\Delta U$.

items: Define the system (the gas) and draw its boundary.
List every heat and work crossing, and give each a sign.
Write Q - W = Delta U and simplify for adiabatic or constant-volume cases.
For an ideal gas use Delta U = m cv Delta T and solve for the unknown.

blocks.title: Do not mix conventions
blocks.text: Some textbooks write $Q+W=\Delta U$ with $W$ done ON the system. This course uses $Q-W=\Delta U$ with $W$ done BY the system. State the convention and be consistent.

blocks.title: Work and heat are not properties
blocks.text: Only the change in internal energy depends on the end states. A system cannot be said to 'contain' heat or work, and different paths between the same states can carry different Q and W with the same Q - W.

points: The closed-system first law is Q - W = Delta U, with Q into the system and W done by the system positive.
For an adiabatic process the work done on a gas raises its internal energy, and for an ideal gas the final temperature follows from m cv Delta T.
For a constant-volume process no boundary work occurs, so Q = Delta U = m cv Delta T.

questions.stem: A gas in a closed piston-cylinder receives 30 kJ of heat and does 12 kJ of work on the piston. What is the change in its internal energy?

options.text: +42 kJ
-18 kJ
+18 kJ
-42 kJ

distractorRationale.a: Adds work instead of subtracting it.
distractorRationale.b: Reverses the sign of the result.
distractorRationale.d: Reverses the signs of both terms.

questions.explanation: With heat in positive and work by the system positive, delta U = Q - W = 30 - 12 = +18 kJ. The gas stores more energy than it gives up as work.

questions.stem: Heat is added to a gas in a rigid, sealed vessel. What does the first law reduce to?

options.text: Q = Delta U, because no boundary work is done
Q = W, because the system is closed
Delta U = 0, because volume is constant
Q = -W, because energy is conserved

questions.correctOptionText: Q = Delta U, because no boundary work is done

distractorRationale.c: Constant volume does not mean constant internal energy.
distractorRationale.d: Work is zero here, not equal to -Q.

questions.explanation: A rigid vessel has no moving boundary, so boundary work is zero. All the heat added therefore appears as an increase in internal energy.

questions.stem: An insulated cylinder of air is compressed, with 50 kJ of work done on the gas. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The internal energy is unchanged because the cylinder is insulated
The internal energy rises by 50 kJ
The internal energy falls by 50 kJ
The heat transfer is +50 kJ

questions.correctOptionText: The internal energy rises by 50 kJ

distractorRationale.c: Work done on the gas increases its energy.
distractorRationale.d: The process is adiabatic, so Q = 0.

questions.explanation: Adiabatic means Q = 0, so delta U = -W. Here W = -50 kJ because work is done on the gas, giving delta U = +50 kJ and a temperature rise for an ideal gas.

questions.stem: If work is defined as positive when done ON the system, which form of the closed-system first law is consistent?

options.text: Delta U = Q - W
Delta U = W - Q
Delta U = Q x W
Delta U = Q + W

distractorRationale.a: That requires W done by the system.

questions.explanation: Work done on the system adds energy, so it must enter with a plus sign. The two forms are equivalent but must not be mixed within one calculation.

questions.stem: The same ideal gas is compressed adiabatically from the same initial state in two ways: reversibly, and irreversibly with friction. In both cases the work input is 25 kJ. How do the final temperatures compare?

options.text: Reversible is higher because it is more efficient
Irreversible is higher because friction adds heat
They are equal because delta U = 25 kJ in both cases
Cannot be compared without the pressure ratio

questions.correctOptionText: They are equal because delta U = 25 kJ in both cases

distractorRationale.a: Efficiency is not relevant: the work in is the same.
distractorRationale.b: Friction is already included in the 25 kJ measured at the boundary.
distractorRationale.d: Temperature depends only on delta U for an ideal gas.

questions.explanation: For an adiabatic closed system delta U = work input regardless of how reversible the process is. With the same mass and cv, the same delta U gives the same final temperature, although the final pressure and entropy may differ.

questions.stem: A gas in a cylinder loses 35 kJ of heat to its surroundings while 20 kJ of work is done on it by the piston. Find the change in internal energy in kJ.
questions.explanation: Heat out is Q = -35 kJ and work on the gas is W = -20 kJ in the by-system convention, so delta U = Q - W = -35 + 20 = -15 kJ. The gas loses energy overall.

questions.stem: 0.80 kg of nitrogen at 295 K is compressed adiabatically with 55 kJ of work done on it. Take cv = 0.743 kJ/(kg K) (typical value) and treat nitrogen as an ideal gas. Find the final temperature in K.
questions.explanation: Adiabatic gives delta U = 55 kJ = m cv (T2 - T1), so T2 - T1 = 55/(0.80 x 0.743) = 92.5 K. Hence T2 = 387.5 K.

questions.stem: A rigid 0.50 m$^3$ tank contains air at 200 kPa and 300 K. Using R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K) and cv = 0.718 kJ/(kg K), find the heat that must be added to raise the temperature to 450 K, in kJ.
questions.explanation: The mass is m = pV/(RT) = 200 x 0.50/(0.287 x 300) = 1.1614 kg. With no boundary work, Q = m cv (T2 - T1) = 1.1614 x 0.718 x 150 = 125.1 kJ.

questions.stem: A gas in a piston-cylinder is heated with a burner while the piston rises against a constant load. Write the first law for the gas, state the sign of each term, and explain why the temperature of the gas may still rise although some of the heat goes into work.
markingGuide: Defines the system as the gas, closed
Q - W = Delta U with Q into the system positive and W by the system positive
Q positive (heat in), W positive (expansion, piston rises)
Delta U = Q - W is positive when Q exceeds W
For an ideal gas Delta U = m cv Delta T so T rises when Delta U is positive
Heat is divided between work output and stored internal energy
questions.explanation: The gas gives up part of the heat as work on the piston, but the remainder raises the stored internal energy. As long as Q exceeds W, delta U and hence the temperature of the gas increase.

questions.stem: Explain why, for an ideal gas, the final temperature after adiabatic compression depends only on the work input and not on whether the compression is reversible, and why Q equals the internal energy change for heating at constant volume.
markingGuide: Delta U = m cv (T2 - T1) for an ideal gas with constant cv
Final T depends on W, m, cv, T1 only; reversibility changes the pressure path but not the energy accounting
Constant volume: no boundary work, W = 0
So Q = Delta U = m cv Delta T
questions.explanation: The first law only needs the energy crossing the boundary. Because internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, the same net energy gives the same temperature rise, and in a rigid vessel all the heat goes to internal energy.
